what_changed: Nothing on this site said what a missing government response does not mean. A reader who found a recommendation and read that no response had been tabled could take away that nothing was done about it, and that inference is not available from anything this site holds. A government can act on a recommendation without ever answering the committee - a budget measure, a regulation, an agency's own decision - and it can answer a committee at length and act on nothing. This site measures whether an answer was given and has no view on whether anything was done. That is now stated on the recommendations page and at the head of the Methods page's known limits, together with what the record does establish: the Senate has required a response within three months since 1973 and the House within six since 2010, so a report with no response is a failure to account to the chamber that asked, whatever else happened. what_changed: Three recommendations were published as a committee's and were a party's. In report 16917 the text under Recommendation 1 and Recommendation 2 was the Coalition Senators' dissenting recommendations, not the committee's. The committee's version now holds a contested number outright, a recommendation that opens by naming a party is attributed to that party wherever it sits, and the signature block that had been running on to the end of some recommendations is cut. Across the 824 recommendations taken from reports, 42 named a party without being flagged and now none do, and no recommendation still carries a signature block. what_changed: An external review found the index misplaced the boundary between the committee's words and the government's in roughly one row in six, and that dissenting recommendations were still being published as committees'. Both are confirmed and fixed. Where a response answered with a bare verdict - "Supported.", "Agreed in principle.", "Noted" - the verdict and the whole answer stayed inside the committee's recommendation, and the page then said the response recorded no separate words for it, which was false: 385 rows ended in a government verdict word and 714 carried that sentence. Conversely a recommendation containing the words "the government has" was split there, and the rest of what the committee asked for was published as the government's answer. Both are now zero. On authorship, the pattern required the word "Senators" after a party name, so 60 recommendations opening "The Australian Greens recommend" were published as committees'; the heading above a recommendation was never read, so a dissent that named its author once - "Dissenting Recommendation - Senator Babet" - was invisible; and section headings were recognised in only one word order. Rows naming a dissenting or party author rose from 152 to 228. Where a document marks a dissent only in prose, which no per-row test can reach, every row from it now says the document also carries dissents. The sentence about separate words now says what is true - that this site could not separate them - rather than making a claim about the document.
